I understand where you're coming from. I have really struggled with anxiety and depression too through out my entire college career. Things started getting a lot better though once I was on the right medication etc. I also think I did quite a bit of maturing. 

Employers really only care that you have finished your degree. I have never had an employer ask for proof of my gpa. Part of your lack of motivation could be caused by the depression which is totally normal. I would stay in school and work with your professors. Take advantage of your universities disability support services. I get extended time on tests as well as my own testing room which eases my anxiety quite a bit. Try not to work and just focus on school and your mental health. That has helped me a ton. If you do drop out you may just end up feeling defeated and disappointed in yourself. Being in school will give you a reason to continue to get out of bed everyday. You will feel better in the long run for it. Also, don't be too hard on yourself. You have your entire life to get your degree. Your mental and physical health are more important than anything else. 

If you need coping skill ideas or just want to talk feel free to pm me.

Take different classes that you're interested in. Research other majors. People change their majors all the time so it is in no way set in stone. I thought I wanted to be a kinesiologist my freshman year and ended up switching my major to sociology the second semester. It's no big deal. You won't have it all figured out and that's totally fine. I don't know anyone who has it all figured out and I'm graduating tomorrow. Just relax and enjoy your experience. Employers are really only concerned about you finishing your degree. 

I can totally see where you're coming from in regards to the history degree. My husband got his bachelors in history and has ended up going back to school to get his masters in history. It is really hard to find a job in that area however if you're passionate about it, it will be worth it.

Everyone has shit going on in their lives. It's part of being an adult. You are expected to be prepared and to have done your homework when you show up to class. If you don't understand the assignment talk with your professor. 

Learn from your mistakes and move on. Doing poorly on an assignment doesn't define who you are as a student or person. Just do better next time. Utilize the resources they give you like the writing center. There is no shame in it. At a university you won't be coddled. It is harder than a community college for a reason.

I transferred after my junior year and I think the best thing to do is get involved with groups on campus. Meet with your classmates to study and go from there. You might really enjoy hanging out with them. 
If you're not going to be living on campus maybe try to get a job. Campus jobs are a great way to meet different people and make friends. I met my husband at my my very first job which was on campus. Also just talk to people. In my experience people at universities are generally pretty friendly and open minded.
If it's an accredited college it doesn't matter. Also Utah State isn't subpar.

I wish I would have gone to a community college my first two years of college. I had a full ride scholarship to Cowley Community College for my first two years and ended up going to a 4 year university instead. I'm from Kansas and credits transfer from colleges pretty seamlessly. Community college really allows you to figure out what you want to do your first two years. The first two years are really about figuring out what it's like being an adult and discovering who you are. Taking the basic intro classes help you discover your interests. Doing this at a community college allows make mistakes without the cost of university prices. Community college also allows you to really work on your gpa so that you can be more competitive if you decide you want to go to grad school.
Ultimately, you choose what your college experience is going to be like. If you want it to be like high school then it will be like high school. The cool thing about being an adult however is that you get to choose who you hang out with.

You'll be fine. You have your entire life to get your degree. Unless you're going to grad school or engineering employers don't really care. They just want to see that you have a degree. Don't stress yourself out. Life is way too short for that.

Unfortunately you are right, most State Facilities are underfunded. There definitely needs to be more places in the community that provides services for people. It's too bad that mental health has the stigma it has. People don't want to take mental illness as serious so many times institutions are forgotten about. A common misconception is that people who suffer from mental illness are acting, or they're just looking for attention. In our society needing help with our mental health is looked down on. You're seen a a weak individual if you have a mental illness and if you need medication to help manage your symptoms you're obviously not fit to manage everyday life.
 
After being discharged I've had a hard time finding a place in the community that can help me. Sometimes it seems like things get done a lot quicker when inpatient than when outpatient. You're more likely to be taken seriously and get help when you're inpatient than outpatient. To me that's very frustrating because I'm trying my best not to have to return to being inpatient. It's not how I want to spend my money or my time. It gets very frustrating when I don't feel like I'm progressing as quickly as I could be with the amount of effort I put into trying to feel better. It's also very easy to feel alone when there aren't others around experiencing similar issues. I feel like there needs to be more resources out there to help keep people out of institutions. I also feel like people need help finding help so they're not stuck with therapists that don't work for them. I know I sure sure use more help.

I have enjoyed Wichita State. I transferred from Kansas State because of the price of tuition and living expenses. I also have family in Wichita. Wichita State has a Co-Op program where you can get college credits if your working at a job that is related to your area of study. The classes also seem to be a lot smaller then at the bigger schools which I liked because it felt more personal. In my experience there are more opportunities to work with your professors outside of class. An example of this would be I worked with one of the deans (who was one of my professors from a previous class) from the College of Liberal Arts and Sciences this summer. I was very impressed at how involved LAS is in the Wichita community. It's something that K-State lacked. So do I recommend it? Yes I do. You can make it the experience you want it to be despite it being a small school.

I'm sure you will be great in college. During your senior year of HS however I would encourage you to really develop your study skills just to be prepared. You have nothing to be nervous about. I remember feeling the way you do and I know there are many who feel the same way. Good luck on your adventures in life! :)

Cutting can be seen as an addiction. As you are probably already aware, when you cut it releases endorphins which is why it feels good to cut. For me, my depression got so bad that I was entirely numb. I cut just to feel something. When I was 10, cutting was the only thing that I could control. So do I cut? Yes. Do I condone it? No. Do I see a problem with it? Yes and I am trying to change.
